docs.title: pinnrl
docs.text:
Physics-informed neural networks for forward and inverse PDE problems, evaluated against numerical references.

A physics-informed neural network (PINN) represents the solution u(x, t) of a PDE as a neural network. It is trained to make the PDE residual, the boundary conditions and the initial condition vanish at sampled collocation points, optionally together with measured data. No mesh is needed, and the PDE's parameters can be learned alongside the solution.

pinnrl packages that workflow:

  • ten PDE configurations: heat (1-D and 2-D), wave, Burgers, convection, KdV, Allen–Cahn, Cahn–Hilliard, Black–Scholes and a damped pendulum. Each exact solution is checked against its PDE, initial condition and boundary conditions by the test suite.
  • seven network architectures;
  • adaptive collocation sampling;
  • adaptive loss weighting;
  • inverse problems (parameter identification);
  • data-driven training on The Well datasets;
  • a Dash dashboard for launching and inspecting runs.
pip install pinnrl
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 2000
pinnrl-dashboard

docs.title: When to use a PINN
docs.text:
Be clear about the trade-off. For a well-posed forward problem in one to three dimensions, classical solvers (finite differences, finite elements, spectral methods) are faster and orders of magnitude more accurate. For the 1-D periodic heat equation with \(\alpha = 0.1\) and \(u_0 = \sin(2\pi x)\), an explicit finite-difference scheme on 100 cells reaches a relative L2 error of about \(6 \times 10^{-4}\) in roughly 30 ms of CPU time; a PINN needs minutes of training to reach about \(10^{-2}\).

PINNs earn their place elsewhere:

Situation Why a PINN helps Inverse problems Unknown coefficients or fields are learned jointly with the solution from sparse, noisy measurements. There is no adjoint code to write. Physics plus data Measurements and conservation laws enter the same loss, so gaps in the data are filled by the physics. Awkward geometry or many dimensions It is mesh-free: points are sampled, not meshed. Differentiable surrogates The trained network is a smooth function of (x, t) that is cheap to evaluate and differentiate.

The long-term goal of the project is the first row applied to industry: digital twins that estimate unmeasured states of real process equipment. See Applications and the Research program.

docs.title: Applications: digital twins
docs.text:
A digital twin is a model of a specific physical asset that is kept in sync with that asset through its sensor data. It is used to estimate what can't be measured, to forecast, and to test decisions before applying them. Most industrial twins today are either detailed simulators that are too slow or too rigid to calibrate continuously, or data-driven models that don't respect physics and extrapolate poorly.

PINNs sit between the two. They combine the conservation laws you already know with the sensor streams you already have, and they solve the inverse problem of learning unknown parameters, closures and hidden states as part of training. That is the gap this project targets.

docs.title: What a PINN-based twin is, and isn't
docs.text:
• It is an estimation layer. It sits above the control system (PLC/DCS), reads the historian or OPC UA, and returns estimates with uncertainty and advisory setpoints. It does not replace real-time control loops.
  • It is not a faster CFD. When the physics is fully known and all you need is a forward simulation, use a classical solver.
  • It earns its keep where something important is unmeasured or unknown: a fouling layer, a drying-kinetics curve, a permeability field, a tissue property. Credible deployment also needs a classical baseline (Kalman filters, moving-horizon estimation) for comparison, and calibrated uncertainty.

docs.title: First target: food-powder lines
docs.text:
The first concrete application is the dairy and food-powder line: evaporators feeding spray dryers, as in cheese- and milk-powder plants. The plan:

  1. falling-film evaporator fouling, estimated from effect-level temperatures and flows;
  2. a spray-dryer soft sensor for residual moisture, with a stickiness-margin advisory;
  3. a coupled line-level twin with measurement design (deciding when to pull a lab sample).

This is the research program; its experiments live in experiments/ (track J of the backlog).

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text: pinnrl-benchmark has two parts: classical baselines, so PINN accuracy has a reference point, and a multi-seed study that compares collocation samplers fairly. Every number below can be reproduced with the commands shown.

docs.title: Classical baselines
docs.text:
pinnrl-benchmark fdm --pde heat     # explicit finite differences, periodic 1-D heat
pinnrl-benchmark fdm --pde wave     # leap-frog, periodic 1-D travelling wave

Both report the relative L2 error at the final time against the analytical solution, plus the maximum error and the wall time. On the default heat problem (\(\alpha = 0.1\), \(u_0 = \sin 2\pi x\), 101 points), the explicit scheme reaches a relative L2 error of about \(7 \times 10^{-4}\) in about 30 ms. The convergence is second order: doubling the points at a fixed diffusion number cuts the error about four-fold. That's the bar a PINN is measured against on forward problems.

docs.title: Reference solutions
docs.text:
When there is no closed form, PINNs are scored against high-accuracy numerical references (pinnrl.benchmarks.reference):

Reference Method Verification burgers_reference Cole–Hopf integral evaluated by a log-sum-exp trapezoid rule Reproduces Basdevant et al. (1986): \(u_x(0, 1.6037/\pi) = -152.00516\) for \(\nu = 0.01/\pi\); agrees with a fine finite-difference solve to \(7 \times 10^{-5}\) allen_cahn_reference Second-order finite differences plus adaptive Runge–Kutta (method of lines) on a grid 8× finer than the output Grid-converged: doubling the solver grid changes the field by less than \(10^{-5}\) (relative)

docs.title: Sampling study (experiments B01 and B06)
docs.text:
pinnrl-benchmark sampling --seeds 10 --steps 15000 --checkpoints 50 --workers 4

Setup: - The Burgers (\(\nu = 0.01/\pi\)) and Allen–Cahn (\(u_t = 0.001\,u_{xx} + 5(u - u^3)\), \(u_0 = x^2\cos\pi x\)) benchmarks. - A tanh MLP (4 × 64) trained for 15,000 Adam steps on 1,000 points, with 10 paired seeds (identical initial weights across samplers). - Five samplers: - uniform and stratified, with fresh points every step; - uniform refreshed every 100 steps, a control for how often points change; - RAD (k = 1, c = 1) and the RL bandit, also every 100 steps. - Each run records the relative L2 error and the residual evaluations spent, including the sampler's own (RAD +20 %, bandit +0.3 %). Samplers are compared at equal steps (B01) and at equal total evaluations (B06).

PDE Sampler Rel. L2, equal steps vs uniform (paired) Rel. L2, equal evaluations vs uniform Burgers uniform 0.055 – 0.055 – stratified 0.038 6/10, p = 0.63 0.038 6/10, p = 0.63 RAD 0.136 3/10, p = 0.11 0.090 2/10, p = 0.06 RL bandit 0.117 1/10, p = 0.06 0.105 2/10, p = 0.01 (worse) Allen–Cahn uniform 0.568 – 0.568 – RAD 0.533 10/10, p = 0.002 0.547 10/10, p = 0.002 RL bandit 0.520 10/10, p = 0.002 0.518 10/10, p = 0.002

Errors are medians over 10 seeds; "6/10" counts the seeds on which the sampler beat uniform; p is from a Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

What this says:

  • Burgers. No sampler is significantly better than uniform. Seed-to-seed variation (6×) and optimizer noise (the error moves 1.7× between checkpoints at a constant learning rate) swamp any sampling effect. Charged its probe cost, the bandit is significantly worse.
  • Allen–Cahn. Adaptive samplers win on every seed and the bandit gets there with about 40 % fewer evaluations early on. But every method stays stuck near the wrong solution (relative error above 0.5).
  • Recommendation: use uniform (or stratified) by default. Use residual_based (RAD) when the solution has sharp features, and measure it against uniform at equal budget. Treat --rl as experimental.

The full write-up, with IQRs, the same-cadence control and the follow-ups it motivates (optimizer settling, resampling frequency, Allen–Cahn failure modes), is in experiments/B01_sampling_equal_compute.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page covers the ideas behind each component of pinnrl: what it does and why it is there. Derivations are in the cited papers.

docs.title: The PINN loss
docs.text:
A network \(u_\theta(x, t)\) is trained to satisfy the PDE \(\mathcal{N}[u] = 0\) together with its boundary and initial conditions (Raissi, Perdikaris & Karniadakis, 2019). Derivatives are computed exactly by automatic differentiation, and the loss is a weighted sum:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = w_r \underbrace{\operatorname{mean}\,\lvert \mathcal{N}[u_\theta] \rvert^2}_{\text{collocation points}} + w_b\,\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary} + w_i\,\mathcal{L}_\text{initial} + w_d\,\mathcal{L}_\text{data} \]

\(\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary}\) averages over every condition on every boundary face, \(\mathcal{L}_\text{initial}\) is taken at \(t = t_0\), and \(\mathcal{L}_\text{data}\) is zero unless observations are attached (inverse and data modes). Each term is a mean squared error with the default loss_function: mse.

Training is ordinary gradient descent on \(\mathcal{L}\). Because nothing ties the network to a mesh, the same code handles irregular domains and higher dimensions. The flip side is that accuracy depends on where the residual is evaluated (sampling), how the terms are balanced (weighting), and what the network can represent (architecture). Those are the three knobs below.

docs.title: Boundary and initial conditions
docs.text:
Kind Enforces Config Dirichlet \(u = g\) on each face dirichlet: {value: 0}, {left: a, right: b}, or {type: exact} (uses the exact solution) Neumann \(\partial u/\partial x_i = g\) on both faces of axis \(i\) (the axis derivative, not the outward normal, so a nonzero \(g\) has the same sign on both faces) neumann: {value: 0} or {type: zero} Periodic \(u\) and \(\partial u/\partial x_i\) match across opposite faces periodic: {}

Every spatial axis gets the condition on both faces. For equations that are second order in time (wave, pendulum), the initial loss also enforces the initial velocity \(u_t(x, t_0)\) (initial_condition.velocity, default 0). Without it the problem is not well posed. Unknown condition types raise an error rather than being silently ignored.

docs.title: Collocation sampling
docs.text:
The residual is only enforced where it is evaluated. Sharp features such as shocks, interfaces and boundary layers occupy a small part of the domain, so uniform points can under-resolve exactly where the error lives.

Strategy Idea Cost uniform A jittered space-time grid, redrawn every batch. Unbiased, and implicitly regularizing. none stratified Latin-hypercube points: one per stratum, so coverage is even. none residual_based (RAD) Draw from a uniform candidate pool (pool_factor = 4 times the batch) with probability \(p(x) \propto \lvert r(x)\rvert^k / \operatorname{mean}\lvert r\rvert^k + c\) (Wu et al., 2023). \(k\) sharpens the focus; \(c\) keeps a uniform floor. The trainer uses \(k = 1\), \(c = 0\); other values are arguments of generate_collocation_points and of the sampling study. one residual evaluation per pool point adaptive (RL bandit, experimental) A DQN with discount 0, i.e. a contextual bandit, learns which of 16 × 8 space-time cells have high residual from probes, and mixes its picks 50/50 with uniform points. 1-D only. 256 residual evaluations (32 cells × 8 points) per update, every probe_every batches (10 in config.yaml)

Adaptive sampling is not free: it has to pay for its overhead and beat a strong uniform baseline at equal budget. Benchmarks reports how the strategies compare.

docs.title: Architectures
docs.text:
Plain MLPs suffer from spectral bias: they learn low-frequency components first and struggle with high-frequency or multiscale solutions (Rahaman et al., 2019). Most of the alternatives exist to counter it.

Key Idea Use it for feedforward Tanh MLP, the standard PINN baseline smooth solutions; the first thing to try resnet MLP blocks with skip connections deeper networks that still train stably fourier Random Fourier features \([\sin(Bz), \cos(Bz)]\) of \(z = (x, t)\) before the MLP, with a fixed \(B_{ij} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) and \(\sigma\) = scale, which sets the frequency band (Tancik et al., 2020); one hidden layer per hidden_dims entry oscillatory or high-frequency solutions siren Layers \(\sin\big(\omega_0 (W z + b)\big)\) with frequency omega_0 (Sitzmann et al., 2020) wave-like solutions; sensitive to omega_0 fno Fourier-neural-operator-style spectral layers applied to point-wise inputs (Li et al., 2021): the FFT runs over each point's hidden features. This is not operator learning: it maps \((x, t)\) to \(u\), not functions to functions. experimentation attention Self-attention blocks over a learned embedding experimentation autoencoder An encoder–latent–decoder MLP experimentation

docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
• Adam is the robust default.
  • L-BFGS is quasi-Newton with a strong-Wolfe line search. Each step works on one sampled batch, so it behaves best with a single batch per epoch (batch_size = num_collocation_points). It often sharpens the final convergence of smooth problems but can stall early.
  • adam_lbfgs runs Adam for a fraction of the epochs (adam_lbfgs_switch_ratio) and then switches to L-BFGS, a common recipe in the PINN literature.
  • Learning-rate schedules: cosine, reduce_lr (on plateau) or constant, with optional linear warmup.

docs.title: Loss weighting
docs.text:
The residual, boundary and initial terms can differ by orders of magnitude in value and in gradient size. When they do, gradient descent effectively ignores the small ones. Fixed weights (loss_weights) are the simplest fix. The adaptive strategies rebalance during training:

  • lrw: gradient-norm balancing. With \(\bar g_i\) a running average (factor alpha) of \(\lVert \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_i \rVert\), the weights are \(w_i \propto 1/(\bar g_i + \epsilon)\), normalized to sum to 1, so no term dominates the update. This is a simplified form of the learning-rate annealing of Wang, Teng & Perdikaris (2021), which scales each term by the ratio of the residual's maximum gradient to that term's mean gradient.
  • rbw: relative loss balancing. The weights are proportional to a running average of each term's loss, normalized to sum to 1 and smoothed again over steps, so the terms with the largest loss get the most weight.

Both replace the loss_weights of the residual, boundary and initial terms; the data weight stays fixed. They are switched off during L-BFGS, where the three terms then have weight 1.

The loss_function setting can be mse (default), mae or huber. The robust losses reduce the influence of outliers, for example noisy observations.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text: Mark PDE parameters as trainable and supply observations. The parameters become torch.nn.Parameters, and a data term \(\mathcal{L}_\text{data} = \operatorname{mean} \lvert u_\theta(x_\text{obs}, t_\text{obs}) - u_\text{obs} \rvert^2\) is added. The parameters enter through the residual (and, for some initial conditions such as the Allen–Cahn and KdV profiles, through the initial loss), so the physics terms pin them to values under which the network solves the PDE, while the data term pulls the solution toward the measurements. Both are optimized together. See Inverse problems.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
A browser app for launching runs, watching them train, and comparing results, with no plotting code to write.

pinnrl-dashboard                       # http://127.0.0.1:8050/, opens a browser tab
pinnrl-dashboard --port 8051 --no-browser

The dashboard lists and writes runs in ./runs/ relative to the directory you start it from, the same folder pinnrl-train uses. Runs launched from the dashboard are ordinary pinnrl-train processes, so they keep going if you close the browser.

docs.title: Live Training
docs.text:
New Training is a form over every pinnrl-train option: PDE, architecture, budget, sampling strategy (including the experimental RL bandit), optimizer, LR schedule, adaptive weights, loss function, and mode. Defaults come from config.yaml for the selected PDE.

  • In inverse mode the form asks for the parameters to identify, their initial guesses, and the observation source: synthetic noisy samples of the exact solution, or an .npz file.
  • Choosing a Well dataset fills in its recommended mode and architecture.

Monitor follows a run as it trains:

  • the loss components and the learning rate;
  • the parameter trajectory in inverse mode, against the true value when known;
  • interactive 3-D surfaces of the predicted u(x, t) and the PDE residual.

The surfaces are read from the run's live_snapshot.npz, which is written every validation_frequency epochs plus at the start and the end. 2-D PDEs are shown as a time slice.

docs.title: Collocation & Solution
docs.text: For a finished run, this tab shows predicted against exact solution surfaces with a time slider, the point-wise error, and where the collocation points were placed over training. That last view is how you check what an adaptive sampler actually did. The exact-solution panel is empty for PDEs without a closed form.

docs.title: Comparison
docs.text:
Select several finished runs to overlay their loss curves and compare final metrics side by side.

Runs can be deleted from the selector (with a confirmation step); only folders inside the runs directory can be removed. To load a run in Python, use pinnrl.training.train.load_run (see Training).

docs.title: Datasets (The Well)
docs.text:
The Well (Polymathic AI, BSD-3) is a collection of large, high-fidelity PDE simulation datasets. pinnrl registers 11 of them. That lets you train neural surrogates on reference data rather than only on analytical toys, and use simulation snapshots as observations.

pip install 'pinnrl[well]'
pinnrl-train --pde heat --dataset active_matter --arch fno --epochs 200 --dataset-steps 9

--dataset sets the mode to the dataset's recommendation (data_only for every registered dataset) unless you pass --mode. --pde is still required, but in data_only mode it is a placeholder: the dataset's domain, dimension and channel count replace the PDE's, and the physics terms are dropped.

Data streams from the Hugging Face mirror (hf://datasets/polymathic-ai/) and is cached in ~/.cache/pinnrl/well; set PINNRL_WELL_CACHE to change that. A run reads the first --dataset-steps time steps of each of --dataset-traj trajectories from --dataset-split. The default is up to 101 steps (the_well's rollout cap) for 2-D datasets and 11 for 3-D ones, which keeps memory and download size in check. The dashboard's launch form has a matching "Time steps" field. It then samples --dataset-points (x, t, u) tuples, with --dataset-seed fixing the sample. Fewer steps means a much smaller download: notebook 04 reads 9 steps, about 26 MB per trajectory instead of about 230 MB.

docs.title: Registered datasets
docs.text:
Domains, time steps and channel counts are taken from each dataset's own files. The spatial domain is the same in every file. dt × steps describes the first training file: five datasets have files that differ. rayleigh_taylor_instability has one file per Atwood number, spanning 29.5 to 118 time units. helmholtz_staircase has one file per frequency, spanning 2.5 to 100. viscoelastic_instability files store 20 or 60 steps. The step size of rayleigh_benard and planetswe varies by up to 1.6 %. A PDE fed by a Well dataset therefore takes its time window from the observations it loads, not from the registry. The run's config.yaml records the window, so load_run rebuilds it without the data.

Name Physics Spatial domain dt × steps active_matter 2-D active nematic fluid [0, 10]² 0.25 × 81 rayleigh_benard 2-D thermal convection [0, 4] × [0, 1] 0.25 × 200 shear_flow 2-D shear flow, Kelvin–Helmholtz roll-up [0, 1]² 0.1 × 200 rayleigh_taylor_instability 3-D buoyancy-driven mixing [0, 1]³ 1.0 × 119 (varies by file) turbulent_radiative_layer_2D 2-D radiatively cooling shear layer [−0.5, 0.5] × [−1, 2] 1.6 × 101 MHD_64 3-D magnetohydrodynamic turbulence [0, 1]³ 0.01 × 100 gray_scott_reaction_diffusion 2-D reaction–diffusion patterns [−1, 1]² 10 × 1001 viscoelastic_instability 2-D elastic turbulence [0, 2π] × [−1, 1] 1.0 × 20 (or 60, by file) acoustic_scattering_maze 2-D acoustic scattering, spatially varying density and sound speed [0, 1]² 0.02 × 202 helmholtz_staircase 2-D Helmholtz (frequency-domain) scattering [−8, 8] × [−0.5, 3.5] 2.0 × 50 (varies by file) planetswe Shallow water on a sphere (colatitude θ, longitude φ in radians; cell centres) θ ∈ [0.009, 3.132], φ ∈ [0, 6.271] 1.0 × 1008

None of these datasets is governed by one of pinnrl's PDE classes. The acoustic and Helmholtz sets involve variable coefficients and a frequency-domain formulation, which the constant-speed wave equation does not represent. Every entry therefore defaults to data_only. euler_multi_quadrants is not registered: its open-boundary files record negative trajectory counts, which the_well 1.2 cannot open, and the periodic variant is not on the mirror.

docs.title: Modes
docs.text:
• data_only: plain regression on the snapshots, which gives a neural surrogate.
  • data_augmented and inverse: the snapshots plus the residual of a PDE (with trainable parameters in inverse). Use these with your own observations of a system that one of the shipped equations actually governs. Passing --mode overrides the dataset's recommendation, so a Well dataset can still be combined with a PDE as an explicit modelling choice, as notebook 04 shows.

From Python, pinnrl.datasets.load_well_slice(name, split, n_traj, n_points, seed, n_steps=...) returns the same {"x", "t", "u"} tensors, usable as PDEConfig.observation_data. Notebook 04 trains an FNO-style network on active_matter end to end.

docs.title: Equations
docs.text:
These are the ten shipped configurations (keys for pinnrl-train --pde). Each shipped exact solution is verified by tests/unit_tests/test_physics_consistency.py: it must satisfy the PDE, the initial condition and the boundary conditions up to float32 round-off (relative residual below 1e-4, initial-condition error below 1e-6). Burgers uses the Cole–Hopf solution, evaluated numerically, and the pendulum a high-accuracy ODE integration. The Allen–Cahn x2_cos benchmark has no closed form and is scored against a numerical reference.

Key PDE Where it arises What makes it hard for a PINN heat, heat_2d \(u_t = \alpha abla^2 u\) Heat conduction, diffusion of species, the pricing kernel behind Black–Scholes Little; the baseline. High-frequency initial data decays fast and is easy to under-resolve. wave \(u_{tt} = c^2 abla^2 u\) Acoustics, vibrating strings and membranes, electromagnetics Second order in time, so it needs the initial velocity. Energy is conserved, so errors don't damp out. burgers \(u_t + u\,u_x = u\,u_{xx}\) A 1-D model of fluid flow and shock formation; traffic flow For small \( u\) a near-discontinuous shock forms. The canonical test for adaptive sampling. convection \(u_t + \mathbf{v}\cdot abla u = 0\) Transport of heat, mass or pollutants by a flow It looks trivial, but PINNs fail for large \(v\) (Krishnapriyan et al., 2021). Information only travels along characteristics. kdv \(u_t + \alpha\,u\,u_x + eta\,u_{xxx} = 0\) Shallow-water waves, plasma waves; solitons A third derivative, and a localized pulse that must move at exactly the right speed. allen_cahn \(u_t = \varepsilon^2 abla^2 u + r\,(u - u^3)\) Phase separation in alloys, image segmentation Thin interfaces of width \(\sim\varepsilon\), with fast dynamics and metastable states. cahn_hilliard \(u_t = M\, abla^2 ig(u^3 - u - \kappa\, abla^2 u ig)\) Spinodal decomposition, polymer blends, battery electrodes Fourth order, mass-conserving and stiff, with fine-scale structure. black_scholes \(V_ au = frac12 \sigma^2 S^2 V_{SS} + r S V_S - r V\), with \( au\) the time to maturity European option pricing A kink in the payoff at the strike; spatial and temporal scales that differ by orders of magnitude. pendulum \( heta'' + b\, heta' + (g/L)\sin heta = 0\) A nonlinear oscillator: mechanics, control, robotics An ODE posed as a PINN. Long time horizons accumulate phase error.

docs.title: Shipped defaults
docs.text:
The defaults in config.yaml are each PDE's domain, parameters and recommended architecture. Override them with flags or your own config.

Key Domain × time Parameters BC IC Architecture heat [0, 2] × [0, 10] α = 0.01 periodic \(\sin(2\pi x)\) (frequency: 2 periods on [0, 2]) fourier heat_2d [0, 1]² × [0, 5] α = 0.01 Dirichlet 0 \(\sin(2\pi x)\sin(2\pi y)\) fourier wave [0, 1] × [0, 1] c = 1 Dirichlet 0 \(\sin(\pi x)\), at rest siren burgers [−1, 1] × [0, 1] ν = 0.01 Dirichlet 0 \(-\sin(\pi x)\) resnet convection [0, 2] × [0, 1] v = 1 periodic \(\sin(\pi x)\) fourier kdv [−15, 15] × [0, 5] α = 6, β = 1 Dirichlet 0 soliton, c = 1 siren allen_cahn [−1, 1] × [0, 1] ε = 0.1, r = 1 exact kink \(\tanh\big(\sqrt{r}\,x/(\sqrt2\,\varepsilon)\big)\) fourier cahn_hilliard [−1, 1] × [0, 1] M = 1, κ = 0.01 exact + Neumann 0 kink \(\tanh\big(x/\sqrt{2\kappa}\big)\) resnet black_scholes S ∈ [0, 200] × τ ∈ [0, 1] σ = 0.2, r = 0.05 exact call payoff \(\max(S-K, 0)\), K = 100 feedforward pendulum t ∈ [0, 10] g = 9.81, L = 1, b = 0.1 periodic in a dummy \(x\) (θ depends on t only) θ0 = 0.5 rad, at rest resnet

The Allen–Cahn and Cahn–Hilliard defaults start from their stationary kinks, which makes them consistency checks rather than hard dynamics problems. The dynamic Allen–Cahn benchmark (as in Wu et al., 2023) is \(u_t = 0.001\,u_{xx} + 5(u - u^3)\) on \(t \in [0, 1]\), with \(u_0 = x^2\cos(\pi x)\) and \(u(\pm 1, t) = -1\). pinnrl-benchmark sampling runs it in rescaled time \(\tau = 5t\), that is \(\varepsilon^2 = 0.0002\), \(r = 1\) and \(\tau \in [0, 5]\). To set it up yourself, use initial_condition: {type: x2_cos}, boundary_conditions: {dirichlet: {value: -1}} and exact_solution: {} (the default exact BCs come from the kink), and score against pinnrl.benchmarks.reference.allen_cahn_reference.

docs.title: Python API
docs.text:
The same pieces the CLI uses. This trains a small network on the 1-D heat equation and scores it against the exact solution:

import torch

from pinnrl.config import Config, ModelConfig, TrainingConfig
from pinnrl.neural_networks import PINNModel
from pinnrl.pdes import HeatEquation, PDEConfig
from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

device = torch.device("cpu")
training = TrainingConfig.from_dict({
    "num_epochs": 200,
    "batch_size": 500,
    "num_collocation_points": 500,
    "num_boundary_points": 100,
    "num_initial_points": 100,
    "optimizer_config": {"learning_rate": 5e-3, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    "scheduler_type": "constant",
    "early_stopping": {"enabled": False},
})

# u_t = alpha * u_xx on [0, 1] x [0, 1], periodic in x, u(x, 0) = sin(2 pi x)
pde = HeatEquation(PDEConfig(
    name="Heat Equation",
    domain=[[0.0, 1.0]],
    time_domain=[0.0, 1.0],
    parameters={"alpha": 0.1},
    boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
    initial_condition={"type": "sine", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    exact_solution={"type": "sin_exp_decay", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    dimension=1,
    device=device,
    training=training,
))

config = Config()
config.device, config.training = device, training
config.model = ModelConfig.from_architecture(
    "fourier",
    {"hidden_dims": [64, 64, 64], "mapping_size": 32, "scale": 4.0, "activation": "tanh"},
    input_dim=2,
    output_dim=1,
)
model = PINNModel(config, device=device)

PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device).train(progress=False)
metrics = pde.validate(model)
print(f"relative L2 error: {metrics['l2_error']:.2e}")

validate returns the relative L2 error \(\lVert u - u^* \rVert / \lVert u^* \rVert\) as l2_error, plus mse, max_error and mean_error.

docs.title: Inverse problems
docs.text:
A forward problem asks for u(x, t) given the PDE and its parameters. An inverse problem asks for the parameters given measurements of u. Examples include a material's thermal diffusivity from temperature traces, a wave speed from surface seismograms, a fouling resistance from evaporator temperatures, or a volatility from option prices.

Classical approaches need a forward solver run many times, plus its adjoint for gradient-based methods (ensemble Kalman filters avoid the adjoint at the cost of an ensemble of solves). A PINN learns the solution and the parameters in one optimization. The parameters become trainable tensors, and a data term joins the physics loss:

\[ \mathcal{L} = w_r\,\mathcal{L}_\text{residual} + w_b\,\mathcal{L}_\text{boundary} + w_i\,\mathcal{L}_\text{initial} + w_d \operatorname{mean} \lvert u_\theta(x_\text{obs}, t_\text{obs}) - u_\text{obs} \rvert^2 \]

The residual ties the parameters to physically consistent solutions; the data term pulls the solution toward the measurements.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinnrl-train --pde heat --arch fourier --epochs 3000 --device cpu \
  --mode inverse --identify alpha --initial-guess alpha=0.5 \
  --obs-points 200 --obs-noise 0.01

Without --obs-path, observations are sampled from the PDE's exact solution at the configured (true) parameters, with Gaussian noise. That makes it a recovery test whose answer is known. The run's metadata.json records the true and recovered values. Any scalar parameter of the PDE can be identified, and --identify can be repeated.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
import torch

from pinnrl.config import Config, ModelConfig, TrainingConfig
from pinnrl.neural_networks import PINNModel
from pinnrl.pdes import HeatEquation, PDEConfig
from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

device = torch.device("cpu")
training = TrainingConfig.from_dict({
    "mode": "inverse",
    "num_epochs": 1500,
    "batch_size": 256,
    "num_collocation_points": 256,
    "optimizer_config": {"learning_rate": 5e-3, "weight_decay": 0.0},
    "scheduler_type": "constant",
    "early_stopping": {"enabled": False},
    "gradient_clipping": 0.0,
    "loss_weights": {"residual": 1.0, "boundary": 10.0, "initial": 10.0, "data": 50.0},
})

pde = HeatEquation(PDEConfig(
    name="Heat Equation",
    domain=[[0.0, 1.0]],
    time_domain=[0.0, 1.0],
    parameters={"alpha": 0.05},                      # the truth, used for synthetic data
    boundary_conditions={"periodic": {}},
    initial_condition={"type": "sine", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    exact_solution={"type": "sin_exp_decay", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 1.0},
    dimension=1,
    device=device,
    training=training,
    trainable_parameters=["alpha"],
    parameter_initial_guesses={"alpha": 0.5},        # start 10x off
))
pde.generate_synthetic_observations(n_points=200, noise_std=0.005, seed=0)

config = Config()
config.device, config.training = device, training
config.model = ModelConfig.from_architecture(
    "fourier",
    {"hidden_dims": [64, 64, 64], "mapping_size": 32, "scale": 4.0, "activation": "tanh"},
    input_dim=2,
    output_dim=1,
)
model = PINNModel(config, device=device)
PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device).train(progress=False)
print(pde.get_trainable_parameter_values())          # notebook 05 recovers about 0.0499

docs.title: Your own measurements
docs.text: Provide an .npz file with arrays x of shape (N, d), t of shape (N, 1) and u of shape (N, 1). Pass it with --obs-path, in the dashboard (Observation source → File), or as PDEConfig(observation_data={"path": ...}). A Well dataset can also serve as the observation source.

docs.title: When the inversion is well posed
docs.text:
• The data must excite the parameter. Diffusivity can't be recovered from a steady state, because it leaves no signature there. Observations must cover the regime where the parameter acts.
  • Balance the data weight. If it's too small, the parameter barely moves from its initial guess. If it's too large, the network fits the noise and the physics stops constraining it. The example above (256 collocation points, 200 observations, noise 0.005) uses 50; 10–100 is a reasonable range to search.
  • Check identifiability before trusting a number. Several parameters, or a parameter field, may not be uniquely determined by the sensors you have. Studying this systematically is part of the research program.

docs.title: Research program
docs.text:
Objective: estimate unknown physics (parameters, coefficient fields, closures and hidden states of a real system) from its routine sensors, with uncertainty you can trust. The first application is digital twins of food-powder lines, meaning evaporators and spray dryers (see Applications).

Inverse modelling is the method. An estimate of unknown physics is only useful if three things hold:

  • the problem is identifiable: the sensors determine the unknowns;
  • it is well conditioned and stable: small disturbances in the data give small changes in the estimate;
  • the uncertainty is calibrated: a 95 % interval contains the truth about 95 % of the time.

The program establishes those conditions on problems with known answers before applying them to plant equipment.

docs.title: How it is organized
docs.text:
• Papers: experiments/PAPERS.md is the paper backlog: 27 papers in four tiers, each with its question, contribution, prerequisite papers, target venues and status.
  • Experiments: experiments/BACKLOG.md lists the 150 experiments behind them, tracks A–K. Track K holds the 50 conditioning, stability and UQ baselines for Tier 1. Each one runs in its own experiments/<ID>_<slug>/ folder with its question, setup, result and conclusion.
  • Rules for every result:
  • equal budgets with the method's own overhead counted;
  • paired seeds (five for main claims), reported as median and IQR with a Wilcoxon test;
  • a classical baseline wherever one exists (finite differences, Kalman filters, moving-horizon estimation, adjoint methods);
  • stated validity conditions.

docs.title: The four tiers
docs.text:
Tier Papers What it establishes 0: foundations P01 audit · P02 sampling at equal compute · P03 optimizers and loss balancing · P04 architectures · P05 failure modes · P06 software (JOSS) Trustworthy defaults and a fair benchmark protocol 1: inverse modelling P07 identification baseline · P08 identifiability and conditioning · P09 training ill-conditioning · P10 disturbance and stability · P11 stability constants and error estimates · P12 high-dimensional stability · P13 calibrated UQ · P14 model-form error and fields · P15 PINN vs classical estimators · P16 physics as a data multiplier When unknown physics can be recovered, how stable the answer is, and how good its error bars are 2: process units P17 evaporator simulator · P18 fouling identifiability · P19 online fouling estimation · P20 drying-kinetics closures · P21 moisture soft sensor · P22 wiped-film evaporators The Tier 1 methods applied to one unit at a time, against simulators with known truth 3: line-level twins P23 coupled-line uncertainty · P24 measurement design · P25 predictive advisory · P26 plant validation · P27 position paper The coupled line, sensor design and validation on real data

How the tiers depend on each other:

  • Tier 0 fixes the defaults every later paper uses.
  • Tier 1 supplies the theory and the tools: conditioning diagnostics, stability analysis and uncertainty quantification.
  • Tier 2 applies them to one unit at a time.
  • Tier 3 starts only after the Tier 2 estimators beat their classical baselines.

  • [x] One training loop (PDETrainer.train / train_steps), one PDE registry, one entry point per action.
  • [x] A working, experimental RL bandit sampler; RAD with k/c.
  • [x] Numerical reference solutions. Done: Burgers reproduces Basdevant et al. (1986), \(u_x(0, 1.6037/\pi) = -152.00516\) for \(\nu = 0.01/\pi\); the Allen–Cahn solution is grid-converged.

docs.title: v0.5: the inverse-modelling core (now)
docs.text:
The goal is to estimate unknown physics with known validity conditions and calibrated uncertainty. Diagnostics come before UQ methods, because an unidentifiable or ill-conditioned problem has no meaningful error bar.

  1. Theory pages. Well-posedness and conditional stability; structural vs practical identifiability; the Bayesian view (loss = negative log-posterior, data weight = 1/σ²); sources of uncertainty; calibration; the numerical-analysis bridge (Lax equivalence, stability constants, PINN error estimates). They're built around the maintainer's reference papers, cited by DOI. Done when: docs/theory/ pages are published and every later module cites the condition it relies on.
  2. Identification baseline. Scalar parameters vs noise, sensors, initial guess and data weight. Done when: F01–F05 are written up (paper P07).
  3. pinnrl.analysis: conditioning diagnostics. The sensitivity Jacobian \(J = \partial y / \partial \theta\) by autograd; Fisher information \(F = J^\top \Sigma^{-1} J\); singular values, condition number and sloppy directions; profile likelihood; the loss-Hessian / NTK spectrum. Done when: K01, K03 and F07 run on heat, KdV and Burgers (P08, P09).
  4. Disturbance and stability analysis. Perturbation suites for data (noise, bias, dropout, delay) and for the problem (IC, BC, parameters); a comparison with the linear prediction \(\delta\theta \approx F^{-1} J^\top \Sigma^{-1} \delta y\); empirical stability constants. Done when: K05–K07 are written up (P10, P11).
  5. pinnrl.uq: calibrated uncertainty. A likelihood-based data term (σ sets the weight); deep ensembles; a Laplace approximation that reuses the Fisher matrix; coverage, width and CRPS metrics. Done when: F06/K10 report calibrated intervals (P13).
  6. Sampling follow-ups for P02. B02 (more PDEs), B03 (the RAD k, c grid), B04 (resampling frequency), B08 (point-count scaling). Done when: P02 can be drafted.

docs.title: v0.6: richer unknowns and inputs
docs.text:
• Field-valued unknowns: a learnable coefficient field \(\alpha(x, t)\) or closure \(f(u)\), with positivity and monotonicity constraints. Done when: \(\alpha(x)\) is recovered on heat (F09, P14).
  • Coupled multi-field systems (output_dim > 1) with per-field BCs and loss weights. Done when: a two-field reaction–diffusion test passes.
  • Measured inputs: BCs and forcing from interpolated time series. Done when: the heat BCs can be driven by a CSV.
  • Sensor operators: point, boundary and integral observations with per-sensor noise and delay. Done when: F05 and K02 use them.
  • Non-dimensionalization helpers (a reference scale per variable). Done when: J01 trains without hand-scaling.
  • High-dimensional stability: dimension sweeps of stability constants and quadrature error. Done when: K08 is written up (P12).

docs.title: v0.7+: process twins
docs.text:
• pinnrl.process: evaporator and spray-dryer models with method-of-lines reference simulators and linearized-stability checks (J01, J07, K09; P17).
  • Classical estimators on the same models: EKF/UKF and moving-horizon estimation (J05; P15, P19).
  • Historian adapter: CSV or Parquet plus a tag map to sensor definitions.
  • A dashboard "Process" view: soft-sensor trends with uncertainty bands, and time to the next cleaning.
  • Bayesian measurement design for sensors and lab sampling (J09; P24).
  • Type checking (mypy) across the package.

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text: A hosted service and monetization (until the research results justify it); a custom PDE-builder UI; operator learning beyond the existing FNO-style layers.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
pinnrl-train --pde <key> --arch <architecture> [options]

Unset options come from the packaged config.yaml: its training block, the chosen architectures entry, and the PDE's block in pde_configs. Pass --config my.yaml to use your own.

Group Flags Problem --pde (key or display name), --arch (feedforward, resnet, fourier, siren, fno, attention, autoencoder), --config, --device (cpu, mps, cuda; falls back to CPU) Budget --epochs, --batch-size, --collocation-points, --boundary-points, --initial-points, --lr Sampling --collocation-distribution (uniform, stratified, residual_based); --rl for the experimental bandit sampler (1-D) Optimizer --optimizer (adam, lbfgs, adam_lbfgs), --lr-scheduler (cosine, reduce_lr), --weight-decay, --gradient-clipping, --early-stopping (on, off) Loss --adaptive-weights (off, lrw, rbw), --loss-function (mse, mae, huber), --huber-delta Mode --mode (forward, inverse, data_only, data_augmented) Inverse --identify NAME (repeatable), --initial-guess NAME=VALUE, --obs-path file.npz, --obs-points, --obs-noise Datasets --dataset NAME, --dataset-split, --dataset-traj, --dataset-points, --dataset-seed, --dataset-base

Examples:

# Burgers with residual-based adaptive sampling and Adam followed by L-BFGS
pinnrl-train --pde burgers --arch fourier --epochs 3000 \
  --collocation-distribution residual_based --optimizer adam_lbfgs

# 2-D heat with gradient-balanced loss weights
pinnrl-train --pde heat_2d --arch fourier --adaptive-weights lrw

Each run is saved in ./runs/<timestamp>_<PDE display name>_<arch>_<rl|no_rl>/, with the dataset name in place of the PDE for a Well run (see Getting started). Early-stopping patience is counted in epochs; validation runs every validation_frequency epochs.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
PDETrainer is the only training loop. The CLI, the dashboard, the notebooks and the benchmarks all use it.

from pinnrl.training import PDETrainer

trainer = PDETrainer(model, pde, config=config, device=device)

# Epoch-based, with validation, early stopping, the LR schedule and run files:
history = trainer.train(num_epochs=2000, experiment_dir="runs/my_run")

# Step-based, for studies: fixed steps or a time budget, no I/O
out = trainer.train_steps(num_steps=5000, resample_every=100)
print(out["steps"], out["train_time_s"], out["loss"][-1])

Each train() call plans its own schedule: the learning rate restarts from training.learning_rate, and the cosine period and adam_lbfgs switch epoch follow that call's num_epochs. trainer.history holds per-epoch entries, including loss_weights when adaptive weighting is on.

train_steps performs exactly the same update as train. It accepts sample_fn(model, progress) -> (x, t) to plug in any sampler, and checkpoints/on_checkpoint to evaluate along the way.

To reload a finished CLI or dashboard run:

from pinnrl.training.train import load_run

pde, model, config = load_run("runs/20261023_120000_Burgers Equation_fourier_no_rl")
print(pde.validate(model)["l2_error"])

docs.title: Choosing settings
docs.text:
• Start with feedforward or fourier, Adam at 1e-3, and uniform sampling. Change one thing at a time.
  • Badly scaled loss terms are the most common silent failure: the boundary or initial loss stalls while the residual drops. Try --adaptive-weights lrw, or raise loss_weights.boundary and loss_weights.initial.
  • adam_lbfgs usually improves the last digit on smooth problems. It rarely rescues a run that Adam got wrong.
  • For problems with sharp features, compare residual_based against uniform at the same budget (see Benchmarks); don't assume it helps.

Grid coordinates flattened to (nx * nt, 1) columns, ij order.

Source code in pinnrl/benchmarks/reference.py 
def flat_points(self) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]:
    """Grid coordinates flattened to ``(nx * nt, 1)`` columns, ``ij`` order."""
    xx, tt = np.meshgrid(self.x, self.t, indexing="ij")
    return xx.reshape(-1, 1), tt.reshape(-1, 1)

docs.title: relative_l2
docs.text:
relative_l2(u_pred)

||u_pred - u||_2 / ||u||_2 over the grid.

Source code in pinnrl/benchmarks/reference.py 
def relative_l2(self, u_pred: np.ndarray) -> float:
    """``||u_pred - u||_2 / ||u||_2`` over the grid."""
    u_ref = self.u.reshape(-1)
    diff = np.asarray(u_pred).reshape(-1) - u_ref
    return float(np.linalg.norm(diff) / np.linalg.norm(u_ref))

docs.title: burgers_reference
docs.text:
burgers_reference(
    nu=0.01 / np.pi,
    nx=256,
    nt=101,
    t_max=1.0,
    n_quad=6001,
    z_max=15.0,
)

Burgers u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx on [-1, 1] with u0 = -sin(pi x).

Cole-Hopf gives

u(x, t) = -∫ sin(pi (x - η)) f(x - η) G(η, t) dη / ∫ f(x - η) G(η, t) dη

with f(y) = exp(-cos(pi y) / (2 pi nu)) and the heat kernel G. Substituting η = sqrt(4 nu t) z turns G into exp(-z²); the integrand is periodic times Gaussian, so the trapezoid rule converges spectrally. z_max = 15 keeps the far peaks of f (which dominate near x = 0 once the shock forms) inside the window.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nu float

Viscosity. The default is the classic 0.01 / pi benchmark.

0.01 / pi nx int

Number of spatial grid points on [-1, 1].

256 nt int

Number of time grid points on [0, t_max].

101 t_max float

Final time.

1.0 n_quad int

Trapezoid nodes on [-z_max, z_max].

6001 z_max float

Half-width of the quadrature window in z.

15.0

def burgers_reference(
    nu: float = 0.01 / np.pi,
    nx: int = 256,
    nt: int = 101,
    t_max: float = 1.0,
    n_quad: int = 6001,
    z_max: float = 15.0,
) -> ReferenceSolution:
    """Burgers ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on ``[-1, 1]`` with ``u0 = -sin(pi x)``.

    Cole-Hopf gives

        u(x, t) = -∫ sin(pi (x - η)) f(x - η) G(η, t) dη / ∫ f(x - η) G(η, t) dη

    with ``f(y) = exp(-cos(pi y) / (2 pi nu))`` and the heat kernel ``G``.
    Substituting ``η = sqrt(4 nu t) z`` turns ``G`` into ``exp(-z²)``; the
    integrand is periodic times Gaussian, so the trapezoid rule converges
    spectrally. ``z_max = 15`` keeps the far peaks of ``f`` (which dominate
    near ``x = 0`` once the shock forms) inside the window.

    Args:
        nu: Viscosity. The default is the classic ``0.01 / pi`` benchmark.
        nx: Number of spatial grid points on ``[-1, 1]``.
        nt: Number of time grid points on ``[0, t_max]``.
        t_max: Final time.
        n_quad: Trapezoid nodes on ``[-z_max, z_max]``.
        z_max: Half-width of the quadrature window in ``z``.

    Returns:
        The reference field on the ``(nx, nt)`` grid.
    """
    x = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, nx)
    t = np.linspace(0.0, t_max, nt)
    u = burgers_cole_hopf(x[:, None], t[None, :], nu, n_quad=n_quad, z_max=z_max)
    return ReferenceSolution(x=x, t=t, u=u)

def allen_cahn_reference(
    epsilon: float = np.sqrt(0.0002),
    t_max: float = 5.0,
    nx: int = 257,
    nt: int = 101,
    refine: int = 8,
    boundary_value: float = -1.0,
) -> ReferenceSolution:
    """Allen-Cahn ``u_t = eps² u_xx + u - u³`` on ``[-1, 1]``, ``u0 = x² cos(pi x)``.

    Dirichlet ``u(±1, t) = boundary_value``. The defaults are the
    ``u_t = 0.001 u_xx + 5 (u - u³)`` benchmark on ``t ∈ [0, 1]`` rewritten
    in the time variable ``τ = 5 t``, which matches the reaction coefficient
    of :class:`pinnrl.pdes.allen_cahn.AllenCahnEquation`.

    The solver grid is ``refine`` times finer than the output grid and the
    output points are a subset of it, so no interpolation error enters.

    Args:
        epsilon: Interface parameter in the residual ``u_t - eps² u_xx - u + u³``.
        t_max: Final time.
        nx: Output spatial points on ``[-1, 1]``.
        nt: Output time points on ``[0, t_max]``.
        refine: Solver-grid refinement factor relative to the output grid.
        boundary_value: Dirichlet value at both ends.

    Returns:
        The reference field on the ``(nx, nt)`` grid.
    """
    n_fine = (nx - 1) * refine + 1
    x_fine = np.linspace(-1.0, 1.0, n_fine)
    dx = x_fine[1] - x_fine[0]
    t = np.linspace(0.0, t_max, nt)
    eps2 = epsilon**2

    u0 = x_fine**2 * np.cos(np.pi * x_fine)

    def rhs(_t: float, v: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray:
        full = np.concatenate(([boundary_value], v, [boundary_value]))
        u_xx = (full[2:] - 2.0 * full[1:-1] + full[:-2]) / dx**2
        return eps2 * u_xx + v - v**3

    sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0.0, t_max), u0[1:-1], t_eval=t, method="RK45", rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-11)
    if not sol.success:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Allen-Cahn reference solve failed: {sol.message}")

    u_fine = np.empty((n_fine, nt))
    u_fine[0, :] = boundary_value
    u_fine[-1, :] = boundary_value
    u_fine[1:-1, :] = sol.y
    return ReferenceSolution(x=x_fine[::refine], t=t, u=u_fine[::refine, :])

def run_sampling_study(
    pdes: Sequence[str] = STUDY_PDES,
    strategies: Sequence[str] = STUDY_STRATEGIES,
    seeds: Sequence[int] = tuple(range(10)),
    settings: StudySettings | None = None,
    workers: int = 1,
    on_result: Callable[[StudyRun], None] | None = None,
) -> list[StudyRun]:
    """Run every ``(pde, strategy, seed)`` combination.

    Tasks are ordered by PDE, then seed, then strategy, so the strategies for
    one seed run side by side under similar machine load. ``workers > 1`` uses a spawn-based
    process pool; ``workers = 1`` runs inline.

    Args:
        pdes: Subset of :data:`STUDY_PDES`.
        strategies: Subset of :data:`STUDY_STRATEGIES`.
        seeds: Seeds to run; each fixes the initial weights.
        settings: Shared study settings.
        workers: Parallel worker processes.
        on_result: Optional callback invoked as each run finishes.

    Returns:
        One :class:`StudyRun` per combination, in task order.
    """
    settings = settings or StudySettings()
    for name in pdes:
        if name not in _PDE_BUILDERS:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown pde {name!r}. Supported: {STUDY_PDES}")
    for name in strategies:
        if name not in STUDY_STRATEGIES:
            raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy {name!r}. Supported: {STUDY_STRATEGIES}")

    references = {name: build_reference(name) for name in pdes}
    tasks = [
        (pde, strategy, seed, settings, references[pde])
        for pde in pdes
        for seed in seeds
        for strategy in strategies
    ]

    results: list[StudyRun] = []
    if workers <= 1:
        for task in tasks:
            run = run_study_case(*task)
            results.append(run)
            if on_result:
                on_result(run)
        return results

    with ProcessPoolExecutor(max_workers=workers, mp_context=mp.get_context("spawn")) as pool:
        for run in pool.map(_worker, tasks):
            results.append(run)
            if on_result:
                on_result(run)
    return results

def run_study_case(
    pde_name: str,
    strategy: str,
    seed: int,
    settings: StudySettings,
    reference: ReferenceSolution,
    device: torch.device | None = None,
) -> StudyRun:
    """Train one PINN for ``settings.num_steps`` steps under one sampler."""
    if pde_name not in _PDE_BUILDERS:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown pde {pde_name!r}. Supported: {STUDY_PDES}")
    if strategy not in STUDY_STRATEGIES:
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown strategy {strategy!r}. Supported: {STUDY_STRATEGIES}")
    chunk = settings.chunk
    if chunk * settings.n_checkpoints != settings.num_steps or chunk % settings.resample_every:
        raise ValueError(
            "num_steps must split into n_checkpoints chunks that are each a multiple "
            f"of resample_every (got {settings.num_steps}, {settings.n_checkpoints}, "
            f"{settings.resample_every})."
        )
    device = device or torch.device("cpu")

    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    pde = _PDE_BUILDERS[pde_name](device)
    trainer = _build_trainer(pde, settings, device)
    torch.manual_seed(seed + 10_000)  # sampling stream, independent of the init

    overhead = {"evals": 0}
    progress = {"value": 0.0}
    sampler = _make_sampler(strategy, pde, settings, device, overhead)
    resample_every = 1 if strategy in _EVERY_STEP else settings.resample_every

    def sample_fn(model, _chunk_progress):
        return sampler(model, progress["value"])

    run = StudyRun(pde_name, strategy, seed, float("nan"), 0, 0.0, 0)
    for _ in range(settings.n_checkpoints):
        out = trainer.train_steps(
            num_steps=chunk, sample_fn=sample_fn, resample_every=resample_every
        )
        run.steps += out["steps"]
        run.train_time_s += out["train_time_s"]
        progress["value"] = run.steps / settings.num_steps
        run.residual_evals = run.steps * settings.n_collocation + overhead["evals"]
        run.curve_step.append(run.steps)
        run.curve_time_s.append(run.train_time_s)
        run.curve_evals.append(run.residual_evals)
        run.curve_rel_l2.append(_relative_l2(trainer.model, reference, device))
    run.rel_l2 = run.curve_rel_l2[-1]
    return run

def summarize(runs: Sequence[StudyRun], budget: str = "steps") -> list[StudySummary]:
    """Median/IQR per ``(pde, strategy)`` plus a paired comparison against ``uniform``.

    ``budget="steps"`` compares final errors (equal training points).
    ``budget="evals"`` compares each run at the last checkpoint whose residual
    evaluations (training plus sampler overhead) do not exceed the smallest
    total spent by any run on that PDE.
    """
    from scipy.stats import wilcoxon

    if budget not in ("steps", "evals"):
        raise ValueError(f"budget must be 'steps' or 'evals', got {budget!r}")
    cap: dict[str, int] = {}
    if budget == "evals":
        for run in runs:
            cap[run.pde] = min(cap.get(run.pde, run.residual_evals), run.residual_evals)

    by_key: dict[tuple[str, str], dict[int, tuple[float, float]]] = {}
    for run in runs:
        point = _at_budget(run, cap.get(run.pde))
        by_key.setdefault((run.pde, run.strategy), {})[run.seed] = point

    summaries: list[StudySummary] = []
    for (pde, strategy), seed_vals in sorted(by_key.items()):
        errors = np.array([v[0] for v in seed_vals.values()])
        baseline = by_key.get((pde, "uniform"), {})
        paired = sorted(set(seed_vals) & set(baseline))
        wins = sum(seed_vals[s][0] < baseline[s][0] for s in paired)
        p_value = float("nan")
        if strategy != "uniform" and len(paired) >= 5:
            diffs = [seed_vals[s][0] - baseline[s][0] for s in paired]
            if any(d != 0 for d in diffs):
                p_value = float(wilcoxon(diffs).pvalue)
        summaries.append(
            StudySummary(
                budget=budget,
                pde=pde,
                strategy=strategy,
                n=len(errors),
                median_rel_l2=float(np.median(errors)),
                q25_rel_l2=float(np.percentile(errors, 25)),
                q75_rel_l2=float(np.percentile(errors, 75)),
                median_time_s=float(np.median([v[1] for v in seed_vals.values()])),
                wins_vs_uniform=wins if strategy != "uniform" else 0,
                p_vs_uniform=p_value,
            )
        )
    return summaries

def solve_heat_1d(
    alpha: float = 0.1,
    frequency: float = 1.0,
    domain: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 1.0),
    t_max: float = 1.0,
    nx: int = 101,
    nt: int = 4001,
) -> FDMResult:
    """Explicit-Euler FDM solver for the 1-D heat equation on a periodic domain.

    Solves ``u_t = α·u_xx`` with initial condition ``sin(2π·f·x)`` and
    periodic boundaries. The defaults give a diffusion number
    ``r = α·dt/dx² ≈ 0.26``, about half the explicit-stability cap of 0.5.

    Args:
        alpha: Thermal diffusivity.
        frequency: Spatial frequency of the sinusoidal initial condition.
        domain: Spatial domain ``(x_min, x_max)``.
        t_max: Final time.
        nx: Number of distinct points on the periodic grid (``dx = (x_max - x_min) / nx``).
        nt: Number of time levels including ``t = 0`` (``nt - 1`` steps).

    Returns:
        :class:`FDMResult` containing the full solution grid, the analytical
        solution at ``t_max``, and L2/max error metrics.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the explicit-Euler scheme would be unstable for the
            chosen ``(nx, nt, alpha)``.
    """
    x_min, x_max = float(domain[0]), float(domain[1])
    # Periodic grid: x_max is the same point as x_min, so it is excluded.
    x = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, nx, endpoint=False, dtype=np.float64)
    t = np.linspace(0.0, t_max, nt, dtype=np.float64)
    dx = (x_max - x_min) / nx
    dt = t_max / (nt - 1)
    r = alpha * dt / (dx**2)
    if r > 0.5:
        raise ValueError(
            f"FDM heat scheme unstable: r = α·dt/dx² = {r:.3f} > 0.5. "
            f"Increase nt (currently {nt}) or decrease nx (currently {nx})."
        )

    u = np.zeros((nt, nx), dtype=np.float64)
    u[0] = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * frequency * x)

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for n in range(nt - 1):
        # Periodic stencil via np.roll: u_xx ≈ (u[i+1] - 2u[i] + u[i-1]) / dx²
        lap = np.roll(u[n], -1) - 2.0 * u[n] + np.roll(u[n], 1)
        u[n + 1] = u[n] + r * lap
    wall = time.perf_counter() - start

    u_exact_final = _heat_exact(x, t_max, alpha, frequency)
    err = u[-1] - u_exact_final
    return FDMResult(
        u=u,
        u_exact_final=u_exact_final,
        x=x,
        t=t,
        l2_error=float(np.linalg.norm(err) / np.linalg.norm(u_exact_final)),
        mse=float(np.mean(err**2)),
        max_error=float(np.max(np.abs(err))),
        wall_time_s=wall,
    )

def solve_wave_1d(
    c: float = 1.0,
    domain: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 1.0),
    t_max: float = 1.0,
    nx: int = 201,
    nt: int = 4001,
) -> FDMResult:
    """Leap-frog FDM solver for the 1-D wave equation on a periodic domain.

    Solves ``u_tt = c²·u_xx`` with the travelling-wave initial condition
    ``u(x, 0) = sin(2πx)``, ``u_t(x, 0) = -2π·c·cos(2πx)`` so that the
    closed-form solution is the right-moving wave ``sin(2π(x − c·t))``. This
    is not :class:`pinnrl.pdes.wave_equation.WaveEquation`'s standing-wave
    exact solution, which starts at rest.

    Args:
        c: Wave speed.
        domain: Spatial domain ``(x_min, x_max)``.
        t_max: Final time.
        nx: Number of distinct points on the periodic grid (``dx = (x_max - x_min) / nx``).
        nt: Number of time levels including ``t = 0`` (``nt - 1`` steps).

    Returns:
        :class:`FDMResult` containing the full solution grid, the analytical
        solution at ``t_max``, and L2/max error metrics.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the leap-frog CFL condition ``c·dt/dx ≤ 1`` is violated.
    """
    x_min, x_max = float(domain[0]), float(domain[1])
    # Periodic grid: x_max is the same point as x_min, so it is excluded.
    x = np.linspace(x_min, x_max, nx, endpoint=False, dtype=np.float64)
    t = np.linspace(0.0, t_max, nt, dtype=np.float64)
    dx = (x_max - x_min) / nx
    dt = t_max / (nt - 1)
    cfl = c * dt / dx
    if cfl > 1.0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"FDM wave scheme violates CFL: c·dt/dx = {cfl:.3f} > 1. "
            f"Increase nt (currently {nt}) or decrease nx (currently {nx})."
        )

    u = np.zeros((nt, nx), dtype=np.float64)
    u[0] = np.sin(2.0 * np.pi * x)
    # First step from u_t(x, 0) = -2πc·cos(2πx). Taylor expansion:
    #   u(x, dt) ≈ u(x, 0) + dt·u_t + 0.5·dt²·u_tt   with u_tt = c²·u_xx
    u_t0 = -2.0 * np.pi * c * np.cos(2.0 * np.pi * x)
    lap0 = np.roll(u[0], -1) - 2.0 * u[0] + np.roll(u[0], 1)
    u[1] = u[0] + dt * u_t0 + 0.5 * (cfl**2) * lap0

    start = time.perf_counter()
    for n in range(1, nt - 1):
        lap = np.roll(u[n], -1) - 2.0 * u[n] + np.roll(u[n], 1)
        u[n + 1] = 2.0 * u[n] - u[n - 1] + (cfl**2) * lap
    wall = time.perf_counter() - start

    u_exact_final = _wave_exact(x, t_max, c)
    err = u[-1] - u_exact_final
    return FDMResult(
        u=u,
        u_exact_final=u_exact_final,
        x=x,
        t=t,
        l2_error=float(np.linalg.norm(err) / np.linalg.norm(u_exact_final)),
        mse=float(np.mean(err**2)),
        max_error=float(np.max(np.abs(err))),
        wall_time_s=wall,
    )

@classmethod
def from_dict(cls, cfg: dict[str, Any]) -> "TrainingConfig":
    """Build from the ``training:`` block of ``config.yaml``.

    This is the one place the YAML layout is translated into a
    ``TrainingConfig``; both :class:`Config` and ``pinnrl-train`` use it.
    ``learning_rate`` and ``weight_decay`` come from ``optimizer_config``
    (or the top level); the scheduler from ``scheduler_type``,
    ``warmup_epochs`` and ``reduce_lr_params``; a legacy ``pde`` key in
    ``loss_weights`` is renamed to ``residual``. Missing keys fall back to
    defaults. Float fields are coerced with ``float()`` because YAML 1.1
    reads ``1e-7`` (no decimal point) as a string.
    """
    optimizer_cfg = cfg.get("optimizer_config", {})
    early_stopping = cfg.get("early_stopping", {})
    reduce_lr = cfg.get("reduce_lr_params", {})
    adaptive = cfg.get("adaptive_weights", {})
    lbfgs = cfg.get("lbfgs", {})

    loss_weights = cfg.get("loss_weights")
    if loss_weights is not None and "pde" in loss_weights:
        loss_weights = dict(loss_weights)
        loss_weights["residual"] = loss_weights.pop("pde")

    return cls(
        num_epochs=cfg.get("num_epochs", 10000),
        batch_size=cfg.get("batch_size", 128),
        num_collocation_points=cfg.get("num_collocation_points", 1000),
        num_boundary_points=cfg.get("num_boundary_points", 100),
        num_initial_points=cfg.get("num_initial_points", 100),
        learning_rate=float(
            optimizer_cfg.get("learning_rate", cfg.get("learning_rate", 0.001))
        ),
        weight_decay=float(optimizer_cfg.get("weight_decay", cfg.get("weight_decay", 0.0001))),
        gradient_clipping=float(cfg.get("gradient_clipping", 1.0)),
        early_stopping=EarlyStoppingConfig(
            enabled=early_stopping.get("enabled", True),
            patience=early_stopping.get("patience", 100),
            min_delta=float(early_stopping.get("min_delta", 1e-4)),
        ),
        learning_rate_scheduler=LearningRateSchedulerConfig(
            type=cfg.get("scheduler_type", "cosine"),
            warmup_epochs=cfg.get("warmup_epochs", 0),
            min_lr=float(reduce_lr.get("min_lr", 1e-6)),
            factor=float(reduce_lr.get("factor", 0.5)),
            patience=reduce_lr.get("patience", 50),
        ),
        collocation_distribution=cfg.get("collocation_distribution", "uniform"),
        adaptive_weights=AdaptiveWeightsConfig(
            enabled=adaptive.get("enabled", False),
            strategy=adaptive.get("strategy", "rbw"),

@classmethod
def from_architecture(
    cls,
    architecture: str,
    arch_cfg: dict[str, Any],
    input_dim: int,
    output_dim: int,
) -> "ModelConfig":
    """Build from one entry of the ``architectures:`` block of ``config.yaml``.

    ``hidden_dim`` and ``num_layers`` default to the first width and the
    length of ``hidden_dims`` when only the list is given (else 128 and 4);
    ``activation`` defaults to ``tanh``. Architecture extras
    (``omega_0``, ``modes``, ...) are copied when present.
    """
    hidden_dims = arch_cfg.get("hidden_dims")
    model = cls(
        input_dim=input_dim,
        hidden_dim=arch_cfg.get("hidden_dim", hidden_dims[0] if hidden_dims else 128),
        output_dim=output_dim,
        num_layers=arch_cfg.get("num_layers", len(hidden_dims) if hidden_dims else 4),
        activation=arch_cfg.get("activation", "tanh"),
        fourier_features=architecture == "fourier",
        fourier_scale=arch_cfg.get("scale", 1.0),
        dropout=arch_cfg.get("dropout", 0.0),
        layer_norm=arch_cfg.get("layer_norm", False),
        architecture=architecture,
    )
    for key in _ARCHITECTURE_EXTRAS:
        if key in arch_cfg:
            setattr(model, key, arch_cfg[key])
    return model

def resolve_device(name: str) -> torch.device:
    """Return ``torch.device(name)`` if that backend is available, else CPU.

    Only ``"cuda"`` and ``"mps"`` are probed; any other name resolves to CPU,
    so a config written on one machine still runs on another.
    """
    if name == "cuda" and torch.cuda.is_available():
        return torch.device("cuda")
    if name == "mps" and torch.backends.mps.is_available():
        return torch.device("mps")
    return torch.device("cpu")

def __init__(self, config: "Config", device=None, **kwargs):
    """Initialize the PINN model.

    Args:
        config: Configuration object with ``model`` and ``device``;
            ``config.model.device`` is set to the chosen device.
        device: Optional device to override config device
        **kwargs: Ignored.
    """
    # Store configuration
    self.config = config

    # Use provided device or get from config
    self.device = device if device is not None else config.device

    # Override device in config with the determined device
    config_with_device = config.model
    config_with_device.device = self.device

    # BaseNetwork reads the ModelConfig through its dict-like .get
    super().__init__(config_with_device)

    # Store architecture type
    self.architecture = config.model.architecture
    self.architecture_name = config.model.architecture  # More accessible name for metadata

    # Create model based on architecture
    if self.architecture == "fourier":
        self.model = FourierNetwork(config_with_device)
    elif self.architecture == "resnet":
        # Create a specific configuration dictionary for ResNet
        resnet_config = {
            "input_dim": config.model.input_dim,
            "hidden_dim": config.model.hidden_dim,
            "output_dim": config.model.output_dim,
            "activation": config.model.activation,
            "dropout": config.model.dropout,
            "device": self.device,
        }

        # Make sure num_blocks is defined, using num_layers as fallback
        if hasattr(config.model, "num_blocks") and config.model.num_blocks is not None:
            resnet_config["num_blocks"] = config.model.num_blocks
        else:
            resnet_config["num_blocks"] = config.model.num_layers

        # Add hidden_dims if defined
        if hasattr(config.model, "hidden_dims") and config.model.hidden_dims is not None:
            resnet_config["hidden_dims"] = config.model.hidden_dims

        self.model = ResNet(resnet_config)
    elif self.architecture == "siren":
        self.model = SIREN(config_with_device)
    elif self.architecture == "attention":
        self.model = AttentionNetwork(config_with_device)
    elif self.architecture == "autoencoder":
        self.model = AutoEncoder(config_with_device)
    elif self.architecture == "fno":
        fno_config = {
            "input_dim": config.model.input_dim,
            "hidden_dim": config.model.hidden_dim,
            "output_dim": config.model.output_dim,
            "num_blocks": getattr(config.model, "num_blocks", None) or config.model.num_layers,
            "modes": config.model.get("modes", 16),
            "activation": config.model.activation,
            "device": self.device,
        }
        self.model = FNONetwork(fno_config)
    else:  # Default to feedforward
        self.model = FeedForwardNetwork(config_with_device)

    # Explicitly move the model to the specified device
    self.model = self.model.to(self.device)
    self.to(self.device)

def __init__(self, config: NetworkConfig) -> None:
    """Initialize the feed-forward network.

    Args:
        config: Network configuration dictionary containing:
            - input_dim: Input dimension
            - hidden_dims: List of hidden layer dimensions
            - output_dim: Output dimension
            - activation: Activation function name ('relu', 'tanh', etc.; default 'relu')
            - dropout: Dropout rate (default 0.1)
            - layer_norm: Whether to use layer normalization (default True)
            - device: Device to place the model on
    """
    super().__init__(config)
    self.input_dim = config["input_dim"]
    self.hidden_dims = config["hidden_dims"]
    self.output_dim = config["output_dim"]
    self.dropout_rate = config.get("dropout", 0.1)
    self.use_layer_norm = config.get("layer_norm", True)
    self.device = config.get("device", torch.device("cpu"))

    # Get activation function name for per-layer instantiation
    activation_name = config.get("activation", "relu")

    # Build layers
    layers = []
    prev_dim = self.input_dim

    for hidden_dim in self.hidden_dims:
        layers.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, hidden_dim))
        if self.use_layer_norm:
            layers.append(nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim))
        # A fresh activation module per layer
        layers.append(self._get_activation_module(activation_name))
        if self.dropout_rate > 0.0:
            layers.append(nn.Dropout(self.dropout_rate))
        prev_dim = hidden_dim

    # Output layer
    layers.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, self.output_dim))

    self.layers = nn.Sequential(*layers)

    # Move model to device
    self.to(self.device)

            - input_dim: Input dimension

            - output_dim: Output dimension

    if "hidden_dim" in config:
        self.hidden_dim = config["hidden_dim"]
    elif (
        "hidden_dims" in config
        and isinstance(config["hidden_dims"], list)
        and len(config["hidden_dims"]) > 0

    elif "num_layers" in config:

    self.dropout = config.get("dropout", 0.1)

                self.dropout,

            for _ in range(self.num_blocks)

        nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim),
        self.activation_fn,
        nn.Dropout(dropout),
        nn.Linear(hidden_dim, in_dim),

def initialize_weights(self) -> None:
    """Draw ``W ~ U(-sqrt(6 / in) / omega_0, sqrt(6 / in) / omega_0)``.

    This is the SIREN hidden-layer rule; it is used for every layer,
    including the first (the paper's first-layer ``U(-1/in, 1/in)`` is not

SpectralConv1d(channels, modes)

Bases: Module

1D spectral convolution layer operating in Fourier space.

Treats the feature/channel dimension as a 1D signal::

X = rfft(x)                                    # (batch, channels // 2 + 1)
Y[:, n] = sum_{m < M} X[:, m] * W[m, n]        # n < M; Y = 0 for n >= M
y = irfft(Y, n=channels)

with M = min(modes, channels // 2 + 1) and W a learnable complex (M, M) matrix (initialised N(0, 1) / (channels * M) per real and imaginary part), so the kept modes are mixed, not scaled one by one.

def __init__(self, channels: int, modes: int):
    super().__init__()
    self.channels = channels
    self.modes = min(modes, channels // 2 + 1)

    # Learnable complex weights: (modes, modes) in complex = (modes, modes, 2) real
    scale = 1.0 / (channels * self.modes)
    self.weights = nn.Parameter(scale * torch.randn(self.modes, self.modes, 2))

def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
    """Apply spectral convolution along the feature dimension.

    Args:
        x: (batch, channels) tensor

    Returns:
        (batch, channels) tensor
    """
    # FFT along feature dimension
    x_ft = torch.fft.rfft(x, dim=-1)  # (batch, channels//2+1) complex

    # Truncate to kept modes
    modes = self.modes
    x_ft_trunc = x_ft[:, :modes]  # (batch, modes)

    # Complex weight multiplication: (batch, modes) x (modes, modes) -> (batch, modes)
    w = torch.view_as_complex(self.weights)  # (modes, modes)
    out_ft = torch.einsum("bm,mn->bn", x_ft_trunc, w)

    # Pad back to full frequency size and IFFT
    out_full = torch.zeros_like(x_ft)
    out_full[:, :modes] = out_ft
    return torch.fft.irfft(out_full, n=self.channels, dim=-1)

def forward(self, x: Tensor) -> Tensor:
    """Forward pass of the layer.

    Args:
        x: Input tensor of shape (batch_size, dim)

    Returns:
        Output tensor of shape (batch_size, dim)
    """
    residual = x
    batch_size = x.shape[0]

    # Use unsqueeze to add sequence length dimension of 1
    # Shape: (batch_size, 1, dim)
    x = x.unsqueeze(1)

    # Linear projections
    q = self.query(x).view(batch_size, 1, self.heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
    k = self.key(x).view(batch_size, 1, self.heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)
    v = self.value(x).view(batch_size, 1, self.heads, self.head_dim).transpose(1, 2)

    # Attention
    scores = torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) * self.scale
    attn = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    attn = self.dropout(attn)

    # Apply attention to values
    out = torch.matmul(attn, v)
    out = out.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(batch_size, 1, self.dim)
    out = self.proj(out).squeeze(1)  # Remove sequence dimension

    # Add residual connection and apply layer norm
    out = self.layer_norm(out + residual)

    return out

def __init__(self, config: NetworkConfig) -> None:
    """Initialize the network.

    Args:
        config: Network configuration dictionary containing:
            - input_dim: Input dimension
            - latent_dim: Latent space dimension
            - hidden_dims: Encoder hidden widths; the decoder uses them reversed
            - output_dim: Output dimension (default 1)
            - activation: Activation function name
            - dropout: Dropout rate (default 0.0)
            - layer_norm: LayerNorm after each hidden linear layer (default True)
    """
    super().__init__(config)
    self.input_dim = config["input_dim"]
    self.latent_dim = config.get("latent_dim", 16)
    self.hidden_dims = config.get("hidden_dims", [32, 64])
    activation_name = config.get("activation", "relu")
    self.dropout_rate = config.get("dropout", 0.0)
    self.use_layer_norm = config.get("layer_norm", True)

    self.output_dim = config.get("output_dim", 1)

    # Encoder maps input -> latent; the decoder maps latent -> output_dim
    # for PINN function approximation.
    self.encoder = nn.ModuleList()
    prev_dim = self.input_dim
    for hidden_dim in self.hidden_dims:
        self.encoder.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, hidden_dim))
        if self.use_layer_norm:
            self.encoder.append(nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim))
        self.encoder.append(self._get_activation_module(activation_name))
        if self.dropout_rate > 0.0:
            self.encoder.append(nn.Dropout(self.dropout_rate))
        prev_dim = hidden_dim
    self.encoder.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, self.latent_dim))

    # Decoder: latent -> output_dim (solution value)
    self.decoder = nn.ModuleList()
    prev_dim = self.latent_dim
    for hidden_dim in reversed(self.hidden_dims):
        self.decoder.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, hidden_dim))
        if self.use_layer_norm:
            self.decoder.append(nn.LayerNorm(hidden_dim))
        self.decoder.append(self._get_activation_module(activation_name))
        if self.dropout_rate > 0.0:
            self.decoder.append(nn.Dropout(self.dropout_rate))
        prev_dim = hidden_dim
    self.decoder.append(nn.Linear(prev_dim, self.output_dim))

PDEBase(config, bandit_sampler=None)

Base class for PDEs solved by PINNs.

A subclass provides the physics:

  • :meth:compute_residual — the PDE operator applied to the network.
  • :meth:_create_initial_condition — u(x, t0) for its IC types.
  • :meth:_exact_solution — a closed-form solution, when one exists.
  • time_order = 2 for second-order-in-time PDEs; the initial loss then also enforces u_t(x, t0) = initial_condition["velocity"] (default 0).

The base class owns everything else: derivatives, collocation sampling, boundary conditions and the composite loss. boundary_conditions in the config maps a kind to its options; every spatial axis gets the condition on both faces:

  • dirichlet: {"value": v} or {"left": a, "right": b} (the lower / upper face), or {"type": "exact"} to take values from the exact solution;
  • neumann: {"value": g} — du/dx_axis = g on both faces;
  • periodic: {} — u and du/dx_axis agree on opposite faces.

exact_solution: {} in the config means the problem has no closed-form solution; :meth:exact_solution then returns None.
